content.title: Introduction
section_headings: 3.1. The relationship between mental and cardiovascular health and disease
content.narrative_summary: This introduction defines mental health as an integral component of overall health, referencing WHO definitions and noting the lack of a single agreed definition. It describes a continuum from optimal mental health through mental health conditions and disorders to severe mental illness, outlines the scope of the consensus statement to address mental health across severity levels in relation to cardiovascular disease, and references use of ICD-11 criteria.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Concept of mental health within this consensus statement.
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Diagram illustrating a continuum from Optimal mental health to Mental illness, with nested categories labeled Mental health, Mental health conditions, Mental health disorders, and Severe mental illness.

continuity.reason: Page begins and ends within running section text, indicating continuation across pages.

content.narrative_summary: This page describes the multidirectional interactions between mental health (and mental health conditions) and cardiovascular (CV) health and disease. Key points: positive mental health features are linked to better CV outcomes, while mental health conditions increase CVD risk; acute CV events and chronic CVD worsen existing mental conditions or trigger new ones; the co-occurrence of CVD and mental health conditions can worsen both prognoses; people with mental health conditions often face socioeconomic disadvantages, stigma, and reduced access to diagnostic and treatment efforts, particularly those with severe mental illness (SMI).

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 2
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Mental/cardiovascular health, disease interaction, and future directions
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Circular diagram illustrating bidirectional interactions and risk between mental health and cardiovascular health/disease, with peripheral arrows for increasing awareness and education, screening, and research. An inner cycle shows mental health linked to CV health and mental health conditions linked to cardiovascular disease, both increasing risk. Below, implementation and testing of consensus-based guidance through ACTIVE principles, Psycho-Cardio team, and a stepped care approach lead via an arrow to improved management and better outcomes.

content.title: 3.2. Enduring problems
content.narrative_summary: This section describes multiple enduring problems at the intersection of severe mental illness (SMI), mental health, and cardiovascular disease (CVD), including insufficient awareness among healthcare professionals of the prevalence and impact of mental health conditions on CVD risk; limited appreciation of mental health incidence and prevalence and their effects on quality of life, adherence, and prognosis; inadequate recognition of stigma; lack of systematic screening, evaluation, communication, and management of mental health in routine CV practice; limited research on improving CV health in people with mental health conditions and on promoting mental health and resilience in people with CVD and their families. It also notes little guidance on improving care despite worse outcomes, limited awareness of caregiver needs, and advocates a person-centred, integrated care approach that includes collaboration with mental health professionals. This integrated “Psycho-Cardio team” is depicted in Figure 3.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 3
figures_tables_algorithms.title: The Psycho-Cardio team
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Hexagonal diagram showing integrated care at the centre, surrounded by six professional groups: mental health professionals, nurses, cardiovascular specialists, social workers, primary care team, and other allied professionals.

content.narrative_summary: Section 3.3 outlines the document’s objectives: reviewing evidence on mental and cardiovascular (CV) health associations; raising awareness of this association and stigma; promoting mental health screening and management in people with CVD and mental health conditions; guiding clinical, systemic, and organizational changes; and identifying research gaps. Section 3.4 describes the need for multidisciplinary Psycho-Cardio teams—including CV and mental health professionals and allied staff—to provide holistic care, coordinate with primary care and social services, and address psychosocial determinants. A person-centred approach is emphasised, introducing the ACTIVE principles for integrating mental health in CV care.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 4
figures_tables_algorithms.title: The ACTIVE principles to improve mental health in cardiovascular care
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: ACTIVE is an acronym for six principles: Acknowledge links between mental and cardiovascular health; Check for mental health symptoms at CV visits and CV risk factors during mental health visits; use validated Tools to screen and diagnose mental health conditions; Implement person-centred management with shared decision-making and stepped care; Venture to integrate structural and functional changes for mental health within CV practice; Evaluate needs for educational support and changes in management and outcomes.

content.title: 4. Impact of mental health on the risk of developing cardiovascular disease
section_headings: 3.5. Section summary points and management consensus statements from Section 3
4. Impact of mental health on the risk of developing cardiovascular disease
4.1. Positive mental health states as predictors of better cardiovascular health
content.narrative_summary: This page concludes Section 3 with summary points and consensus statements on integrating mental health into cardiovascular (CV) care. Section 4 introduces the impact of mental health on CV risk in individuals without known CVD, emphasizing robust population-based and meta-analytic evidence for psychosocial stressors as independent predictors of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and mortality. Subsection 4.1 discusses subjective well-being (SWB) – including life satisfaction, optimism, and sexual health – as protective factors linked to lower all-cause mortality, coronary heart disease, and heart failure, and outlines plausible physiological (e.g., autonomic regulation, inflammation reduction) and behavioral mechanisms. Subsection 4.2 defines psychosocial stress as a response to social demands exceeding regulatory capacity, noting its role in CV risk and beginning exploration of stress appraisal processes.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: SECTION SUMMARY POINTS
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Section summary points
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) Mental health and mental health conditions interact with CV health and CVD in a multidirectional way.
(ii) The coexistence of CVD and mental health conditions can create a mutual interaction that worsens both mental and CV health, leading to poorer outcomes.
(iii) Routine CV clinical practice lacks integrated, systematic and appropriate screening, evaluation, communication, and management of mental health.
(iv) There is limited evidence on the best ways to communicate, promote, maintain, and improve mental health and resilience in people with CVD and their family members.
(v) The evidence base to guide practice in relation to the screening and management of mental health conditions in people with CVD is limited.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: MANAGEMENT CONSENSUS STATEMENTS
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management consensus statements
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) Cardiovascular care is optimal if it is person-centred and seeks to improve overall health, not only CV but also mental health, as an integral component.
(ii) A multidisciplinary team including mental health professionals, psychologists, and/or psychiatrists (Psycho-Cardio team) is needed in CV care to provide guidance for practice and appropriate mental health assessment, support, and management to people with CVD and their caregivers.
(iii) Cardiovascular services should aspire to implement a Psycho-Cardio team approach, tailored to the local population, context, and resources.
(iv) Implementing the ACTIVE principles is a practical approach to transform routine clinical CV care towards being more person-centred, integrating mental healthcare into routine CV practice to improve care.

section_headings: 5.2.1.1. Prevalence of depressive symptoms and depression in people with cardiovascular disease
5.2.1.2. Impact of depressive symptoms and depression on cardiovascular disease prognosis
content.narrative_summary: Section 5.2.1.1 reviews that depression is one of the most common mental health conditions in people with cardiovascular disease (CVD), with an estimated global prevalence of 18%. Rates are higher in women and older adults, and depression is associated with modifiable lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol intake, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet) and other CVD risk factors (diabetes, hypertension). Section 5.2.1.2 discusses that depression is a known risk factor for poor cardiovascular prognosis: post-MI depression predicts higher all-cause mortality and more CV events; depression after ACS and PCI is linked to increased mortality; in heart failure, depressive symptoms associate with hospitalizations and mortality; depression at the start of exercise rehabilitation predicts poorer improvement; and depression or suicide attempts before/after heart transplantation may worsen long-term outcomes, possibly due to medication non-adherence.

5.2.3.1. Prevalence of post-traumatic stress disorder in cardiovascular disease
5.2.3.2. Impact of post-traumatic stress disorder on cardiovascular disease prognosis
content.narrative_summary: This page reviews the relationship between psychological conditions—depression, anxiety, and cardiac disease–induced post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD/PTSS)—and outcomes in people with cardiovascular disease (CVD). It highlights that depressive symptoms are linked to poorer self-management, lower adherence to medication, lifestyle modification, and increased risk of adverse events and reduced quality of life. Prevalence of anxiety in CVD patients ranges from about 29% to 34%, with higher rates in women and varying by diagnostic methods. Anxiety has a negative impact on prognosis, including increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events and mortality over long-term follow-up, though its immediate effect post-acute events may be limited. Anxiety may also influence self-care behaviors. Cardiac disease–induced PTSD symptoms are common after acute events or interventions and are associated with increased rates of rehospitalization, mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

section_headings: 5.2.3.3 Impact of post-traumatic stress disorder on self-management and adherence to medical recommendations
content.narrative_summary: The page presents two narrative sections. The first (5.2.3.3) notes that evidence on the impact of cardiac disease–related PTSD on self-management and adherence is mixed, with stronger evidence linking PTSD to non-adherence in medication and physical activity. The second (5.2.4) describes studies showing that loneliness at hospital discharge in people with cardiovascular disease is associated with significantly worse outcomes, including higher all-cause mortality and cardiovascular event risk, and that living alone increases CV risk, whereas being married or widowed is associated with lower risk.

section_headings: 5.3. Addressing the mental health needs of informal caregivers for people with cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: Section 5.2.5 defines chronic stress as ongoing physical and emotional imbalance due to life events and reports it affects 58% of people with CVD. A large observational study found higher perceived stress in women than men and linked chronic stress to poorer quality of life and mental health after MI. The Cardiac Distress Inventory–Short Form identified elevated distress in younger people and women, and high stress in HF patients predicted adverse events. Section 5.3 discusses the role of informal caregivers in supporting lifestyle changes and treatment adherence for people with CVD. Caregiving can produce significant emotional and physical toll, with caregivers of CAD and VAD patients experiencing elevated anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life. A holistic, team-based Psycho-Cardio approach is recommended, and Figure 6 (not shown) outlines specific caregiver support actions.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Table 3
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Prevalence of post-traumatic stress disorder/post-traumatic stress symptoms in people with cardiovascular disease
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Prevalence of PTSD and PTSS by CVD subgroup: ACS/Post-MI – 12% PTSD, 0–26% PTSS depending on measurement; PTSD in 7–20% post-CABG; 28–35% in SCAD survivors. Advanced HF/post-transplantation – 11–19% PTSD post-HTx. ICD recipients – 12–38% PTSD after cardiac arrest; ≥1 appropriate shocks increased PTSD risk (OR 6.0); higher PTSD with electric storms. ACHD – 1–30% PTSD, varying by region and measurement; women and those lacking psychosocial support have higher risk.

section_headings: 5.4. Section summary points and management consensus statements from Section 5
6. Identification, prevention, and management of mental health issues in people with cardiovascular disease
6.1. Awareness of needs in people with cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: This section emphasizes that depression and anxiety are often overlooked in people with CVD despite high prevalence and negative effects on outcomes and adherence. It recommends considering formal mental health screening at a low threshold during clinical encounters, outlines insights from recent patient‐written accounts, and refers to proposed person‐centred support components in Figure 7, highlighting the importance of integrating mental health assessment within CVD care.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 6
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Suggestions for supporting informal caregivers of people living with cardiovascular disease.
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
• Listen: Informal caregivers must be heard as they are an invaluable source of information and often experience much distress
• Reassure: Caregivers should be reassured that they are not alone and that their emotional responses are both valid and important
• Assist: Caregivers need assistance to acquire new knowledge, organize information, follow management instructions, and implement lifestyle changes
• Encourage: Caregivers should be encouraged to access relevant medical and social support, both for the patient and for themselves
• Refer: Caregivers should be referred to relevant services to support their health and social needs

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Section summary points
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Section summary points
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) There is a multidirectional association between CVD and mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, and PTSD, increasing each other’s risk.
(ii) Mental health conditions in people with CVD, such as depression, can negatively affect self-management, including adherence to medication and lifestyle changes, and are associated with worse outcomes.
(iii) The effects of anxiety and PTSD on adherence and CV outcomes are less clear and might be time-dependent.
(iv) Caregivers play an essential role in supporting their family members who cope with CVD to incorporate lasting lifestyle changes and to adhere to treatment plans; assessing and supporting caregivers’ well-being benefits both parties.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Management consensus statements
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management consensus statements
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) It is reasonable to assess depression, anxiety, and PTSD in people with established CVD as they are highly prevalent and impact outcomes, and refer promptly to a professional when needed.
(ii) Chronic stress and loneliness are associated with negative outcomes in people with CVD and should prompt referral if identified during clinical assessment.
(iii) Incorporating informal caregiver well-being assessment and support is advisable in the holistic approach of mental and CV health.

content.narrative_summary: This section emphasizes the importance of taking a clinical history to evaluate mental health symptoms in patients with cardiovascular disease, identifying previously unrecognized or new manifestations that may require education or social support. It highlights considerations for mental health screening: determining who will screen, when screening should occur, which tools to use, and screening frequency. Collaboration with mental health professionals (the Psycho-Cardio team) is recommended to develop protocols for screening and guiding referrals based on severity.

section_headings: 6.2.2. Suggested approach to screening people with cardiovascular disease for psychological distress, depression, and anxiety
content.narrative_summary: The page presents two tables outlining psychometric properties and screening timing/tools for anxiety and depression in cardiovascular patients, followed by narrative emphasizing that mental health conditions in CVD patients can be episodic and should be integrated into routine care. It notes variability in symptom intensity over time, cites a study on new-onset anxiety and depression post-ICD implantation, and discusses the debated value and timing of screening. Section 6.2.2 describes two assessment approaches (diagnostic interview vs questionnaire), advocates questionnaires as practical starting points, and recommends referral based on elevated scores. Section 6.2.3 highlights challenges in heart failure patients, where overlapping symptoms may mask mental health issues and screening timing and interpretation remain unclear.

6.3.1. Communication, education, and support for people with mental health conditions and cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: The page describes the importance of psychosocial assessment for candidates for VAD and HTx, listing key domains: risk factors for poor outcomes, decision-making capacity, environmental resources, and VAD operation capacity. Two assessment tools (PACT and SIPAT) are noted for post-HTx risk prediction but unvalidated in VAD populations. Quality of life and mental health assessment tools, including the WHO-5 questionnaire and disease-specific and generic QoL instruments (e.g., SF-12, EQ-5D), are recommended. Section 6.3 emphasizes management of mental health in cardiovascular disease, highlighting effective communication, empathy, active listening, shared decision-making, and stepwise, patient-centered interventions. A stepped care model (Figure 9) is referenced.

content.narrative_summary: This section describes psychological interventions for people with cardiovascular disease, including cognitive-behavioural therapy, psycho-education, mindfulness-based techniques, internet- and mobile-based solutions as supportive strategies. A psycho-educational approach provides structured knowledge transfer about the illness, integrates emotional and motivational aspects, and is embedded in cardiovascular care settings to improve coping, treatment adherence, and quality of life.

content.narrative_summary: Section 6.3.4 describes social prescribing as a holistic approach connecting people with non-medical community resources—such as arts workshops, group activities, gardening, green exercise, cooking classes, music therapy, and digital platforms—to enhance mental well-being, reduce social isolation, and support adherence to cardiovascular treatment. Evidence from 17 studies (n=5036) shows improvements in mental health, well-being, and quality of life, though more CVD-specific research is needed. Section 6.3.5 summarizes psychological interventions (relaxation, cognitive techniques, emotional support, CBT, exposure therapy) for CHD, CAD, AF, AMI, and CVD patients. Meta-analyses and trials report reductions in cardiovascular mortality, symptom burden, depressive and anxiety symptoms, healthcare use, and hospital admissions, with psychosocial support endorsed by ESC/ERS guidelines.

6.3.8 Physical activity and exercise in people with cardiovascular disease and mental health conditions
6.3.9 Diet and nutrition approaches in cardiovascular disease and mental health conditions
content.narrative_summary: This section reviews evidence for mental health interventions in people with cardiovascular disease. It describes behavioural activation and its comparable efficacy to antidepressants, EMDR and trauma-focused counselling for PTSD symptoms, holistic lifestyle changes, structured physical activity and its psychological benefits, various dietary and nutritional strategies (e.g., Mediterranean diet, fasting interventions, omega-3 supplementation) with preliminary mental health outcomes, and the challenges and benefits of smoking cessation, highlighting the need for further robust clinical trials.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Figure 10
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Pharmacological management of cardiovascular disease and depression, anxiety, or post-traumatic stress disorders
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart outlining management steps: start with screening for people with depression, anxiety or PTSD. For those in remission or with mild symptoms, assess if already on psychotropic therapy; if no, offer psychological support or counselling; if yes, continue medication or re-assessment with considerations for weight gain, diabetes, QTc prolongation, dyslipidaemia. For moderate or severe cases per ICD-11, obtain psychiatric consultation leading to either continuing medication/re-assessment (with same considerations) or initiating new psychotropic/antidepressant medication based on psychiatric symptom severity, treatment benefit, possible interactions, CV side effects, lifetime CVD risk, comorbidities, and patient preferences. Special considerations include introducing SSRIs, SNRIs, or newer antidepressants (excluding esketamine) for up to 4 weeks; gradual benzodiazepine discontinuation if used >1 month; avoiding antidepressants in heart failure except in severe depression. All pathways conclude with assessing and managing CVD risk factors (including medication if needed) and behavioral interventions to support healthy lifestyles.

content.narrative_summary: This page discusses pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions between antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs) and cardiovascular drugs, highlighting cytochrome P450-mediated metabolism, smoking induction of CYP1A2, and the effects of enzyme inhibition by SSRIs and amiodarone, with implications for drug concentrations and bleeding risk. It covers the use of anxiolytics, sedatives, and hypnotics, recommending assessment for switching to SSRIs or CBT for insomnia and noting benzodiazepine risks. In patients with specific cardiovascular conditions, it reviews treatment considerations: avoiding benzodiazepines post-AMI, using bupropion or varenicline for smoking cessation, selecting antidepressants with lower pro-arrhythmic potential in ventricular arrhythmias (e.g., citalopram/escitalopram and avoiding TCAs), and assessing risks vs benefits of antidepressants in heart failure, with SSRIs preferred for fewer CV side effects but with bleeding and QTc concerns.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of the use of antidepressant and psychotropic drugs in heart failure and peri-procedural settings, noting that SSRIs have lower drug-interaction risk due to minimal CYP inhibition, while MAO inhibitors and TCAs are contraindicated in HF. Venlafaxine and duloxetine should be used with caution. Antidepressant use in HF should be restricted to severe cases; diuretics and nitrates carry higher depression risk, whereas beta-blockers, statins, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aspirin, aldosterone antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors do not. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PCI or CABG based on low-quality evidence. Section 6.6 describes fragmented healthcare and novel integrated models for collaborative mental and cardiac care with evidence from RCTs. Section 6.7 introduces summary points.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) Ideally, assessment of mental health status should be performed routinely within CVD clinical practice and implemented when the context of local capacity and capability allows.
(ii) Depression and anxiety can easily be overlooked in the routine care of people with CVD and/or considered ‘normal’ reactions to individual clinical/prognostic burden of disease.
(iii) Clinical history can be used to identify mental health symptoms. If there is clinical suspicion, formal screening with validated tools is advised.
(iv) Psycho-Cardio teams are needed to structure pathways for:

    • Referral;
    • Treatment of people with CVD and suspected or established mental health conditions.
(v) Medical interventions including pharmacotherapy may be needed for people with CVD who are diagnosed with mental health conditions, especially for severe symptoms of depression, anxiety, or PTSD.
(vi) In some people with CVD, combination therapy of psychological interventions plus medication may be useful.

content.title: 7. Severe mental illness and cardiovascular disease
section_headings: 7. Severe mental illness and cardiovascular disease
7.1. Cardiovascular risk in people with severe mental illness
7.2. Prognosis in severe mental illness and cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: Section 7.1 outlines that severe mental illnesses (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, recurrent major depressive disorder) are associated with significantly impaired psychosocial functioning, approximately 14–15 years reduced life expectancy, more than 2.5-fold higher all-cause mortality, and a 2- to 3-fold increased risk of CVD compared with the general population, with a pooled CVD prevalence of 9.9% and adjusted risk particularly elevated in younger adults. Section 7.2 describes that co-occurrence of SMI and CVD increases all-cause mortality and worsens cardiovascular prognosis: up to 2.5-fold higher CHD and CV mortality, lack of decline in post-MI mortality over time in schizophrenia, onset of heart failure seven years earlier, and poorer outcomes after ICD implantation, CRT, VAD, and HTx in people with SMI.

rows.recommendation: Screening of mental health with validated screening tools is advised after a new diagnosis or CV event, at least once during follow-up and anytime based on clinical judgement of need.
Initial simple screening with a two-item measure (i.e. Whooley questions, PHQ-2, GAD-2) can be incorporated into routine practice.
A low threshold for mental health screening in people with CVD is advised, considering the high prevalence of mental health conditions in people with CVD and its impact on outcomes.
Following an abnormal result in the initial screening, a longer validated screening instrument should be used to determine if condition severity is low, moderate, or high.
Psycho-Cardio teams must define who is responsible for the assessment of mental health conditions and how and when it will be done, tailoring it to the specific context and resources.

Each Psycho-Cardio team may choose a particular screening tool after careful assessment of its validity, reliability, and applicability to their population, but standardized screening tools are preferred for mental health assessment.
People scoring high on a screening questionnaire need referral for diagnostic assessment and appropriate treatment by a mental health professional.
Applying a stepped care approach to manage mental health conditions in people with CVD is reasonable based on preferences, severity of symptoms and condition, and resources available.
Developing and evaluating tailored intervention programmes aimed at alleviating distress of people coping with CVD and caregivers may be useful.
Lifestyle measures and psycho-education are useful for all people with CVD while psychological therapies may be helpful for people experiencing depression and/or anxiety.

Cardiac rehabilitation is an opportunity to screen people for depression and anxiety and can contribute to improve mental health after CV events or be an opportunity to identify and manage mental health conditions.
Avoiding benzodiazepines as first-line therapy in the management of anxiety and depression is advised.

Anxiolytics, sedatives, and hypnotics are overused and overprescribed in the general population, especially among the elderly and people with mental health conditions, so careful selection of indications is advisable.
Antidepressant use is advised for those with moderate to severe anxiety disorders and depression under the guidance of qualified mental health professionals.
The use of antidepressants in HF is only advisable in severe depression symptoms where the risk of untreated depression outweighs the risk of taking antidepressants.

In people with ventricular arrhythmias, antidepressants associated with an increased propensity to prolong QTc (such as TCAs and possibly citalopram/escitalopram in dosages over 20 mg), may be switched to newer antidepressants with better safety profiles.

Given the frequent interactions between antidepressants and CV drugs affecting their efficacy and safety, therapeutic drug monitoring is advisable to optimize pharmacotherapy and minimize potential side effects and clinically relevant drug interactions.

section_headings: 7.3. Increased cardiovascular disease risk in people with severe mental illness
content.narrative_summary: The section describes the multifactorial aetiology of cardiovascular disease risk in people with severe mental illness (SMI), including genetic, biological, disease-specific, treatment-specific, lifestyle factors and treatment disparities. Lifestyle and biological risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidaemia, obesity and smoking contribute to higher CV risk in people with SMI. Common genetic vulnerability for schizophrenia and diabetes is noted, as are effects of negative/depressive symptoms leading to sedentary lifestyle. Schizophrenia is associated with more than threefold risk of obesity, metabolic syndrome and diabetes compared with the general population; bipolar disorder shows higher prevalence of hypertension; people with schizophrenia have five times higher odds of smoking and up to 65% are smokers, with higher rates of alcohol addiction. People with SMI have not experienced the same reductions in modifiable risk factors or CVD mortality declines as the general population. Disease-specific and medication-induced risk factors include side effects leading to obesity, diabetes, hyper-triglyceridaemia and hypercholesterolaemia, though the impact of these metabolic side effects on CVD risk is complex and not necessarily independent predictors.

content.narrative_summary: This page continues discussion of cardiometabolic risk management in people with severe mental illness (SMI). It reviews weight-loss advice (BMI≥25 kg/m^2 or waist ≥88 cm in women/≥102 cm in men) and mixed results of behavioural interventions and pharmacotherapies (metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors). Glucose and lipid lab outcomes are reported as secondary assessments; metformin is first-line for antipsychotic-associated weight gain but not universally effective. Smoking cessation strategies mirror general population approaches, combining behavioural and pharmacological therapies (varenicline, bupropion, nicotine replacement), with a note on CYP1A2 induction raising drug levels. Pharmacological management of SMI includes long-term psychotropics with mood stabilizers and anxiolytics; attention is drawn to CYP450 pharmacokinetics and CV side effects via receptor blockade. Section 7.6 outlines CV condition management in SMI: multidisciplinary coordination, adherence to psychotropics, dose minimization, lifestyle modification, and adjunctive therapies (metformin, nicotine replacement), summarized in bullet points. Section 7.6.1 notes increased arrhythmia and SCD risk in SMI.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management of people with cardiovascular disease and severe mental illness
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Flowchart outlining assessment and management of individuals with severe mental illness (SMI) and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Begin by assessing mental health status and cardiovascular risk, then branch based on SMI remission status or severity. For those in remission or with mild symptoms, evaluate adherence to psychiatric and CVD treatment, directing non-adherent individuals to interventions supporting treatment adherence and considering long-acting injectables, and adherent individuals to monitoring of cardiovascular side effects, drug interactions, and therapeutic drug levels. For new or unremitted moderate/severe SMI, refer for psychiatric consultation and psychotropic medication initiation or change, choosing agents with lower metabolic risk, monotherapy if possible, and long-acting injectables to improve adherence. Emphasizes a person-centred multidisciplinary Psycho-Cardio team approach, with ongoing ECG monitoring post-antipsychotic initiation, periodic assessment of risk factors and side effects, adherence monitoring, psycho-education/behavioural counselling, and CVD medication adjustment if needed.

content.narrative_summary: The page reviews the impact of antipsychotic drugs on cardiac electrophysiology in people with severe mental illness. It emphasizes that QTc interval prolongation increases torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death risk, recommending ECG monitoring before and after drug initiation and annually. Definitions and thresholds for acquired long QT syndrome are provided, along with management steps based on QTc values (>500 ms, intermediate prolongation) and avoidance of QT-prolonging drug interactions. Additional reversible causes of QT prolongation, formula selection for QT correction, and measurement challenges are noted. The section on heart rate changes describes sinus tachycardia and bradycardia risks, identifies management options including rate control and drug selection, and highlights lithium’s effects. Finally, clozapine-induced myocarditis and cardiomyopathy risks are discussed, with guidance to discontinue clozapine and refer for cardiology evaluation if suspected.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management of psychotropic drugs with QT interval prolongation properties
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Action and supporting information rows:
- Assess symptoms: typically asymptomatic; in case of torsades de pointes, palpitations, dizziness, syncope, cardiac arrest.
- Diagnostic work-up: 12-lead ECG at baseline and after 1, 6, and 12 weeks; more frequent ECG if QT prolongation; use Fridericia formula for rate correction in tachycardia; check potassium, calcium, magnesium; ambulatory ECG if symptoms; exclude inherited long QT syndrome.
- Management: caution with sertindole, amisulpride, ziprasidone, iloperidone, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine; aim for lowest effective dose; check for QT-prolonging drugs and interactions; correct electrolytes; consult CredibleMeds.org; address reversible factors (e.g., bradycardia, hypothyroidism, starvation, alcohol/substance abuse, ischaemia); note non-reversible factors (heart failure, hypertrophy, atrial fibrillation, hepatic/renal impairment, female sex, age>65 years); individualized risk-benefit if QTc >470 ms.
- Special precautions: stop treatment if QTc >500 ms or increase in QTc 60–70 ms from baseline.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: SECTION SUMMARY POINTS
figures_tables_algorithms.title: Section summary points
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) The presence of SMI increases CV risk, especially in younger people.
(ii) Regular CV risk assessment is essential in people with SMI regardless of age, to prevent the development or progression of CVD, ideally before the prescription of antipsychotics and, afterwards, periodically in all stages of illness.
(iii) Management of CVD in people with SMI aims to reduce modifiable CV risk factors, including weight gain, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking, unhealthy diet, and sedentary lifestyle habits.
(iv) CVD management in people with SMI benefits from optimizing SMI pharmacotherapy: preferring monotherapy; using medications less likely to induce weight gain or other CV risks; monitoring for drug interactions and side effects; ensuring medication adherence.
(v) Efforts to alleviate psychosocial and stress-related factors are needed in people with SMI.

figures_tables_algorithms.title: Management consensus statements
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
(i) Addressing stigma and managing CVD in people with SMI in accordance with CV Guidelines and best clinical practice is a responsibility of all healthcare professionals.
(ii) CV care for people with SMI can be improved by following a holistic person-centred approach, involving close collaboration between the Psycho-Cardio team with psychiatrists, general practitioners, and sometimes other specialists to proactively facilitate the engagement of people with SMI in such programmes.

8.1. Sex and gender differences in mental health and cardiovascular disease
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses how biological sex and sociocultural gender influence incidence, prevalence, presentation, diagnosis, management, and response to treatment in cardiovascular (CV) and mental health conditions. It highlights that depression and anxiety are twice as prevalent in women versus men, have increased more in women over the past two decades, and pose important risk factors for acute coronary syndromes (ACS) and cardiovascular mortality. Women experience greater impact from chronic self-perceived stress and marital stress, whereas men are more affected by job-related stress. Differences in stress response, genetic influences, inflammation, and hormone-related receptor signaling pathways are noted, with evidence drawn from human and animal models.

section_headings: 8.3. Mental health and cardiovascular disease in people with frailty and multimorbidity
8.3.2. Mental health, cardiovascular disease, and multimorbidity
8.3.3. Summary of evidence in older adults with cardiovascular disease and mental disorders
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the increased risk of drug interactions in elderly patients, noting antipsychotics metabolized by the CYP system can interact with cardiovascular medications (e.g., beta-blockers, statins), lithium requires serum and renal monitoring and interacts with diuretics and ACE inhibitors, and benzodiazepines can cause sedation and respiratory depression, especially with other CNS depressants. Polypharmacy heightens risks like QT prolongation, arrhythmias, hypotension, myalgia, myopathy, and creatine kinase elevation. Section 8.3 reviews frailty as diminished physiological reserve overlapping with cardiovascular disease and multimorbidity. Frailty affects 40–80% of heart failure patients and has a pooled prevalence of 19% in ischaemic heart disease, increasing adverse event risk. Comprehensive geriatric assessments, including psychological and socio-environmental domains, are recommended. Depression and anxiety have a bidirectional relationship with frailty, increasing risk over time. Multimorbidity—presence of ≥2 chronic conditions—affects ~40% of the global population and is linked to higher healthcare use and costs. Collaborative management via Psycho-Cardio teams is advocated, although evidence from RCTs (e.g., 3D trial) is mixed: interventions improve mental health outcomes but show limited impact on cardiovascular endpoints. Further research on integrated care models is needed. The summary emphasizes the complexity of managing older adults with CVD, mental health conditions, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy, and highlights the role of non-pharmacological, integrated approaches (see Figure 16).

section_headings: 8.4. Mental health and cardiovascular disease in socioeconomically deprived populations
content.narrative_summary: Individuals with low socioeconomic status (SES) face increased stress, reduced access to healthcare, and limited social engagement, exacerbating psychosocial stress and cardiovascular disease (CVD) progression. Financial or housing instability may amplify stress responses, increasing vulnerability to mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety. Lower SES correlates with unhealthy lifestyle behaviors, higher prevalence of CVD and heart failure, and pronounced disparities in marginalized communities where structural inequalities worsen outcomes. Socioeconomic deprivation influences CV risk estimation, and mental health service utilization following CVD events is more frequent in deprived and ethnically marginalized populations. Health inequities are particularly evident among homeless individuals, those with substance use disorders, sex workers, and the incarcerated, with greater exclusion impacts in females. content.narrative_summary: This section reviews the psychological challenges and cardiovascular implications in people with cancer. It discusses how chronic stress associated with cancer diagnosis and treatment can increase the risk of major cardiovascular events, describes Takotsubo syndrome risk factors, and highlights cancer survivors’ fears of recurrence and associated distress. It also addresses mental health issues in advanced cancer, therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity, the impact of cancer treatments on psychological well-being, and the role of psychological interventions in cardio-oncology care.

content.narrative_summary: The text describes the impact of psychosocial distress—depression, anxiety, anger, social isolation, marital/family distress, sexual dysfunction, and substance abuse—in the cardio-oncology setting and emphasizes multidisciplinary team discussions involving cardiovascular specialists, oncologists, and mental health professionals. It recommends referral to mental health specialists collaborating with the primary cardio-oncology team to provide comprehensive care. A comprehensive approach is advocated, monitoring cardiovascular and mental health during and after cancer therapy, with a cardio-oncology clinic doctor addressing cardiovascular toxicity. Physical activity benefits include exercise-based programmes improving cardiorespiratory fitness and survival in cancer survivors with CVD, ECR-improved depression in breast cancer survivors, exercise interventions reducing mortality and improving psychosocial function and sleep in advanced/metastatic cancer, and comprehensive cardiovascular risk reduction programmes enhancing mental health in women receiving potentially cardiotoxic breast cancer therapies.

section_headings: 8.6. Section summary points and management consensus statements from Section 8
content.narrative_summary: Section 8.5.8 discusses that there are no specific cardio-oncology recommendations for psychiatric drugs, but general cardiology and oncology evidence may be applied with caution. Advanced cancer increases ventricular arrhythmia risk, and psychiatric, cardiovascular, and oncological drugs can interact to prolong QT interval and increase bleeding risk. Avoiding drug–drug interactions is crucial to maintain cancer treatment effectiveness. Treating cancer-related cardiovascular dysfunction and anaemia may alleviate anxiety and dyspnoea, while managing tachyarrhythmias can improve psychological symptoms. Reducing anxiety and stress may also lower blood pressure and help control hypertension in people living with cancer.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Management Consensus Statements
figures_tables_algorithms.title: MANAGEMENT CONSENSUS STATEMENTS
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Three consensus statements advising: (i) Psycho-Cardio teams should tailor interventions to population specifics (sex, age, frailty, SES); (ii) assess antidepressants, drug interactions, and side effects in multimorbid, elderly, frail patients; (iii) proactive programmes for migrants and refugees to address cardiovascular and mental health access.

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Key Messages
figures_tables_algorithms.title: 9. Key messages
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Twelve key messages emphasizing the integration of mental and cardiovascular care, implementation of tailored Psycho-Cardio team approaches, use of ACTIVE principles, screening and stepped care strategies for mental health in CVD, limited evidence on psychosocial intervention outcomes, balanced pharmacotherapy considering drug–drug interactions, support for caregivers, stigma reduction, and personalization based on individual patient characteristics (sex, age, frailty, SES, comorbidities).

figures_tables_algorithms.label: Section Summary Points
figures_tables_algorithms.title: SECTION SUMMARY POINTS
figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Six summary points noting: (i) higher prevalence of depression, anxiety, chronic stress in women with CVD; (ii) worse mental health outcomes in women with CVD; (iii) gender-related biological and sociocultural factors; (iv) importance of evaluating mental health and frailty in elderly CVD patients; (v) socioeconomic deprivation linked to higher CVD and mental disorder rates; (vi) three-way relationships among cancer, CVD, and mental disorders.

content.title: 10. Gaps in knowledge
section_headings: 10.1 Knowledge gaps in relation to prevention and screening
10.2 Knowledge gaps in relation to clinical management
10.3 Knowledge gaps in relation to special populations
10.4 Knowledge gaps in relation to healthcare systems and healthcare delivery
content.narrative_summary: This page outlines the major gaps in understanding and managing the interplay between mental health and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Section 10 emphasizes the lack of evidence-based, cost-effective interventions for prevention, screening, and treatment of mental health conditions in people with CVD, as well as the need for research on optimal screening protocols, tailored non-pharmacological and pharmacological strategies, and the role of pharmacogenomics and psychiatric drugs in cardiac populations. Section 10.3 notes recalibration needs for cardiovascular risk scores in people with severe mental illness. Section 10.4 highlights the need to develop and evaluate integrated care models, streamlined care pathways, and community-level interventions to address socioeconomic disparities. Section 11 concludes by calling for integrated mental and CV health assessment, stigma reduction, co-designed care models, and rigorous randomized controlled trials to evaluate interventions.
